title: How to Calculate Your “Enough Number” for Retirement Based on Real Expenses
description: Bottom-up budgeting to find your true FI number.
content:
The '25x Rule' (saving 25 times your annual spending) is a great heuristic, but it relies on one critical input: your annual spending. Most people guess this number. 'I think I spend $50k.' If you are wrong by $10k, your retirement target is off by $250,000. To have confidence in your retirement plan, you must move from 'Top-Down' estimates to 'Bottom-Up' calculation. By auditing your actual life costs and adjusting for the retirement phase, you can pinpoint your 'Enough Number' with precision.

Key Takeaways

  • Track, Don't Guess: Use 12 months of bank/credit card data to find your true burn rate. Most people underestimate their spending by 20% because they forget 'lumpy' expenses like car repairs and holidays.
  • The Retirement Adjustments: Subtract work costs (commuting, saving). Add retirement costs (health insurance, travel). The number changes.
  • The Tax Wedge: Your spending number is 'Net'. You need to withdraw 'Gross'. If you need $60k to spend, you might need to withdraw $75k to cover taxes. Your portfolio must support the Gross number.
  • The 'Sleep Well' Buffer: Once you calculate the number, add 10%. This buffer handles unknown inflation or bad market returns without forcing you back to work.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Healthcare is the biggest variable. A pre-65 retiree might pay $15k/year for insurance. A post-65 retiree pays much less. Your 'Enough Number' might need to support a higher burn rate for the first few years (The Bridge).

The Bottom-Up Worksheet

Build your budget line by line.

1. Core Expenses (Survival)

Housing (Tax/Ins/Maint), Food, Utilities, Healthcare.
Example: $40,000/year.
Goal: Cover this with Social Security + Guaranteed Income.

2. Discretionary Expenses (Joy)

Travel, Dining, Hobbies, Gifts, Cars.
Example: $20,000/year.
Goal: Cover this with Portfolio Drawdown (Stocks).

3. The Tax & replacement Layer

Add 15% for Taxes. Add $5,000/yr for 'lumpy' replacements (Roof/Car).
Total Gross Need: $75,000/year.

4. The Calculation

Total Need: $75,000.
Social Security: -$30,000.
Portfolio Draw: $45,000.
Enough Number (25x): $45,000 x 25 = $1,125,000.

Stress Testing the Number

  1. The 3.5% Test: What if you live to 100? Divide by 0.035 instead of 0.04. Target becomes $1.28M. It's safer.
  2. The Inflation Test: What if inflation is 5%? You need high equity exposure (stocks) to keep up. Your 'Enough' number must include growth assets, not just bonds.
  3. The 'One More Year' Syndrome: Once you hit the number, it is hard to quit. Set a date. 'When I hit $1.2M, I give 6 months notice.' Don't move the goalposts forever.
  4. Variable Spending: Remember, you can cut travel in a bad market. You have levers. You don't need to save for the worst-case scenario every single year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does my paid-off house reduce the number?

Yes! No mortgage means lower annual expenses. Lower expenses = Lower portfolio needed. A paid-off house is a massive accelerator.

What about Long Term Care?

That is a separate bucket. Either buy insurance or earmark a specific asset (home equity) to pay for it. Do not mix it with your daily living number.

Can I retire on less?

Yes, if you are willing to be flexible. LeanFIRE people retire on $600k by living extremely frugally. Your lifestyle dictates your number.
